core: working definition of normalization: organizing tables to reduce redundancy and keep data consistent (attributed to Microsoft's database documentation)
the problem it solves: duplicated data drifts when a change is made in one place but not another (customer address stored with every order)
the core idea: each fact stored once, in one place
the normal forms named at intuition level: first, second, and third normal form, one line each, no formal math
third normal form as the common practical target
the practical payoff: updates become simpler and safer
normalization vs over-normalization: too many tiny tables is also a problem
honest framing: normalization is a design habit, not a one-time rule
supporting: origin: the idea was proposed by Edgar F. Codd in 1970 as part of his relational model
anomalies caused by unnormalized design: insertion, update, and deletion anomalies
higher normal forms (Boyce-Codd, fourth, fifth) exist but are beyond everyday design
normalization is structural; data accuracy rules belong to the sibling data-integrity topic
outOfScope: data integrity as a discipline (own topic: databases-and-sql:foundations:data-integrity)
relationships and cardinality (own topics: relationships, one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many)
SQL syntax for designing or altering tables (own topics: sql-basics and the SQL family)
formal definitions of functional dependencies and the math of higher normal forms

claims.claim: Normalization is the process of organizing data in a database — creating tables and establishing relationships between them according to rules designed to protect the data and make the database more flexible by eliminating redundancy.
Redundant data creates maintenance problems: when a fact exists in more than one place, every change to the fact must be made in exactly the same way in all locations.
A customer address change is easier to implement if the address is stored only in the customers table and nowhere else in the database.
Each rule of normalization is called a normal form; observing the first three rules places a database in third normal form.

First normal form eliminates repeating groups in individual tables: create a separate table for each set of related data, identify each set with a primary key, and do not use multiple fields in a single table to store similar data.

Second normal form creates separate tables for sets of values that apply to multiple records, relates them with a foreign key, and requires that records depend on nothing other than the table's primary key.
Third normal form eliminates fields that do not depend on the key: values in a record that are not part of the record's key do not belong in the table.
Although other levels of normalization are possible, third normal form is considered the highest level necessary for most applications.
Database normalization was first proposed by British computer scientist Edgar F. Codd as part of his relational model; the first normal form was defined by Codd in 1970.
Unnormalized designs suffer insertion, update, and deletion anomalies; an update anomaly occurs when the same record shows different values (for example, different addresses) on different records.
Perfect normalization is not always practical: normalization requires additional tables, and many small tables may degrade performance or exceed open file and memory capacities.
Normalization reduces data redundancy and improves data integrity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What normalization primarily targets: redundancy alone, or redundancy plus inconsistent dependencies.
positions: Microsoft Learn describes normalization as eliminating redundancy and inconsistent dependency, with both named in the definition.
Wikipedia's lead defines normalization as reducing data redundancy and improving data integrity.
Some short tutorials describe normalization only as 'removing duplicates.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The sources agree that redundancy is the core target; Microsoft Learn adds inconsistent dependency (a fact stored where it does not belong). The lesson states the definition with both redundancy and consistency, and uses the inconsistent-dependency idea in the third-normal-form section without formal terminology.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether third normal form is the endpoint of normalizing or merely a common stopping point.
positions: Microsoft Learn: third normal form is considered the highest level necessary for most applications.
Wikipedia: a relation is informally described as normalized if it meets third normal form, and most 3NF relations are free of the three anomalies; higher forms (BCNF, 4NF, 5NF, 6NF) exist.
Some textbooks present BCNF as the standard classroom target.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents third normal form as the common practical target, while noting that higher forms exist and are special cases — matching both sources without claiming 3NF is the mathematical end of normalization.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft in public/content/phase-2/lessons.json contained no verifiable claims about normalization at all — only generic boilerplate ('Database Normalization is a foundational concept in Databases & Sql', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer'), which was discarded wholesale and replaced with the source-verified lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic machine-generated draft with an original, source-verified lesson; no wording from the draft was retained.
Attributed the working definition to Microsoft's database documentation and the origin of the idea to Edgar F. Codd (1970), per Wikipedia.
Added the over-normalization balance and the honest design-habit framing, both supported by Microsoft Learn's cautions about additional tables and performance.
Kept data integrity, relationships, and foreign keys strictly as references to sibling topics, per the subject's topic boundaries.
